desc:
Write the fraction numerator / denominator as a decimal string.

  • If the fractional part is empty, return just the integer part (2/1 gives "2").
  • If the decimal expansion terminates, return it exactly (1/2 gives "0.5").
  • If it repeats forever, put the shortest repeating block of digits in parentheses, starting from the first digit that begins the repetition (1/3 gives "0.(3)", 1/6 gives "0.1(6)", 4/333 gives "0.(012)").
  • A negative value starts with -; zero is just "0".

The result of every test is a valid, unique string under these rules.
constraints: The result has at most about 5,000 fractional digits
hints: Do long division by hand: the integer part first, then repeatedly multiply the remainder by 10 and divide again to get the next digit.
The expansion ends if a remainder of 0 appears. Otherwise there are fewer than |denominator| different remainders, so some remainder must eventually repeat, and from then on the digits repeat too.

Store, for every remainder you have seen, the position in the digit list where it first occurred. When a remainder shows up again, insert ( at its stored position and ) at the end. Handle the sign and the zero numerator before dividing, using absolute values.
editorial: Work with absolute values and a sign computed from the two operands (no sign for a zero numerator). The integer part is n // d; if the remainder is 0 you are done. Otherwise generate fractional digits by long division: rem *= 10, the next digit is rem // d, and the new remainder is rem % d.

The next digit and all following ones depend only on the current remainder. So the first time a remainder repeats, the digits between its earlier appearance and now form the repeating block. A dictionary from remainder to digit index gives that index in O(1). The loop ends when the remainder becomes 0 (terminating) or repeats, which takes at most |denominator| steps because there are only that many possible remainders.
Use Python integers or 64-bit types in other languages: -231 / -1 overflows 32 bits.
